content.title: Rebuttal for jQQY
content.comment:
Thanks for your constructive and helpful comments!

The benefits of model-based methods: Compared with the model-free setting with function approximation, we emphasize two benefits: 1) Our algorithm does not need Bellman completeness, which is a common requirement for Bellman evaluation operator under the model-free settings; 2) Model-based algorithms are known to be more sample efficient compared to model-free methods, making them useful in applications with relatively small sample size, e.g., medical domains. 3) Studying model-based algorithms also allows us to consider problem-specific estimators and function classes for transition models in different scenarios, e.g., when incorporating prior knowledge from experts is desired. One potential extension of the current work is to study the algorithm under the Bayesian setting in which model-based methods are favored.

Assumptions for model-based algorithms: In the literature of statistical learning, with assumptions of realizability and controlled entropy for the model class, the transition model is learnable with a finite-sample theoretical guarantee. In our work, we analyze theoretical results for the proposed model-based algorithm assuming that the transition model is efficiently learnable, which is formulated in Assumption 2.

content.title: Rebuttal for EAHi
content.comment:
We gratefully appreciate your valuable comment.

Q: Regarding computational efficiency. 

A: Thank you for pointing out this issue. We will do empirical studies in the future. For projected gradient descent, we will consider a more general version that allows the constraint set to be non-convex.

Q: The theoretical analysis of this work seems based on a couple of well-known ingredients. 

A: Thank you for your careful reading. We agree that these parts are studied separately in the existing literature. However, analyzing the theoretical results for the proposed algorithm is not a simple combination of these well-known results. Our work is the first one to theoretically analyze offline model-based actor-critic algorithms with the help of a novel decomposition of suboptimality. We have also studied how distribution shifts coming from two different causes intertwined with each other.

Q: The assumptions seem a bit strange.

A: We would like to clarify that our assumptions are not particularly stronger than the existing literature. The model-based method CPPO only requires one realizability assumption for theoretical guarantees; however, a practical algorithm has not been designed. In other words, designing an implementable algorithm for CPPO would require more assumptions, as in our work. For model-free methods, to the best of our knowledge, most of them need Bellman completeness, which our algorithm does not require.  We admit that the linear approximation of Q in our setting may be restrictive, and we plan to consider more general function classes for Q for updating the policy.

content.title: Rebuttal for ZsBc
content.comment:
Thank you for your careful review and constructive comments.

Q: The claims of the paper do not seem to be supported by the result. 

A: Thank you for pointing out this problem. We plan to study the implementation of the proposed algorithm and do experiments in the future. For projected gradient descent, we will consider a more general version that allows the constraint set to be non-convex.

Q: There are claims about completeness being too strong of an assumption and somehow model realizability is less strong. I think this is inaccurate. Given model realizability, one can construct a complete class by using the models.

A: Thank you for the comment. We were not aware of this result before. Could you please tell us more details or some related literature?

Q: The theoretical techniques do not appear to be that new. It’s more of a combination of existing techniques. While this is not a bad thing, I think it just means more focus should be put on the results.

A: Thank you for your suggestions. Though it looks like a combination of existing techniques, the way of combining them is not trivial, and we proposed a novel decomposition of sub-optimality for offline model-based actor-critic algorithms. We will add more empirical results in the future version.

Q: There is a lot of discussion about why pessimism works, but this has already been explored quite extensively in past work. I think much of this can be made more concise so that the main contributions of the paper are brought forth.

A: Thank you for your suggestions. We will revise our manuscript carefully with the highlight of our contributions.

content.title: Rebuttal for Reviewer vQS5
content.comment:
Thank you for your careful review and constructive comments.

Contributions and novelty: From the theoretical perspective, our work was motivated by CPPO in order to provide an implementable version. They focused more on analyzing the convergence rates of estimators for several transition models, which are roughly summarized in our Assumption 2. Compared to CPPO, our work focuses more on the theoretical guarantee for the proposed implementable algorithm, making the estimations of dynamic models more flexible. We will highlight our novelty in the future. From the computational perspective, we plan to study the implementation of the proposed algorithm and do experiments in the future, as we mentioned in the summary. Investigating theoretical results for Algorithm 2 which incorporates projected gradient descent for a non-convex constraint set would also be set as a future direction.

Empirical evaluation: 
Thank you for pointing out this issue. We agree that empirical evaluation is necessary, and we will set it as our first revising task.

content.title: Summary of Rebuttal
content.comment:
We greatly appreciate all reviewers for their careful review and constructive comments. After consideration of all concerns and suggestions, we plan to withdraw the current manuscript and improve it substantially in the future version. But we still want to address all concerns and questions pointed out by reviewers. We address some common issues here, and then will reply to each reviewer separately regarding their specific concerns with more details.

1. Regarding the lack of empirical studies:
We realize that the lack of empirical studies makes the proposed algorithm less convincing. To this end, we plan to implement the proposed algorithm,  conduct empirical experiments, and compare the proposed algorithm to state-of-the-art methods in the future version.

2. Regarding the motivation for studying model-based algorithms: Model-based algorithms are known to be more sample efficient compared to model-free methods, making them useful in applications with relatively small sample sizes, e.g., medical domains. 
Studying model-based algorithms also allows us to consider problem-specific estimators and function classes for transition models in different scenarios, e.g., when incorporating prior knowledge from experts is desired. One potential extension of the current work is to study the algorithm under the Bayesian setting in which model-based methods are favored.

3. Regarding linear approximations for Q: We consider the linear approximation of the Q-function as a starting point for the purpose of designing a practically implementable algorithm for model-based offline RL with theoretical guarantees. The linear approximation of the Q function allows us to update the policy in a finite-dimensional space for the sake of computational feasibility. Investigating more general forms for approximating Q would be a future direction for us.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes PeMACO (pessimistic model-based actor-critic for offline), an implementable variant of CPPO (constrained pessimistic policy optimization) with PAC guarantee. Compared with CPPO, PeMACO parameterizes the policy as an energy-based class and uses NPG for policy improvement. A more practical implementation of PeMACO is introduce by using projected SGD to solve policy evaluation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
 - PeMACO is with PAC guarantee. 
 - Overall good presentation. 

Weaknesses:
 - Contribution: The paper is motivated by CPPO, since CPPO has PAC guarantee but without a practical implementation. However, algorithm 1 has PAC guarantee and can be practically implemented in terms of policy improvement, but policy evaluation is still a blackbox. I understand that to resolve such an issue, the authors propose algorithm 2, which uses projected SGD to solve policy evaluation. But such a proposal splits the theory (algo 1) and implementation (algo 2), thus downlevels the contribution of the current revision. 
 - Novelty: The paper highly relies on CPPO to motivate the algorithm. In terms of CPPO, the algorithm only tries to adapt the policy improvement/evaluation to a more implementable version. 
 - Empirical evaluation: I believe the motivation for CPPO was for a theoretical understanding of pessimistic model-based offline RL. However, since this paper tries to modify CPPO to an implementable version, some empirical evaluation would be strongly recommended to justfy the efficacy of the method. Without any empirical result, the current algorithm is hard to compare with other SOTAs.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Good. 

Quality: Good. 

Novelty: Fair. 

Reproducibility: I did not check the proof. But based on my understanding I believe the proof should be fine.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a new model-based actor-critic algorithm for offline reinforcement learning. The algorithm selects models in a confidence set so as to underestimate the value function for the critic in order to update the actor. Theoretical results are presented, bounding the sub-optimality of the resulting policy in terms of partial coverage. There are no experiments. The algorithm is designed to be computationally efficient.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- To my knowledge, there have been no other model-based actor critic algorithms theoretically analyzed, as done in this paper.
- The paper is clear and well written.
- The theoretical results seem sound.

Weaknesses:
- The claims of the paper do not seem to be supported by the result. The method is not proven to actually be computationally efficient. It is assumed that (3) can be solved by an oracle, but the solution to this is precisely the hard part of the optimization problem, so I feel too much burden is placed on the oracle to justify computational efficiency. The authors give a short discussion of solving (3) via projected gradient descent, but there is a strong assumption that the value function is convex in the model parameters. It’s not investigated whether this is a reasonable assumption. Even if convexity is not reasonable, experiments showing that it’s still effective could suffice, but these were not presented.
- There are claims about completeness being too strong of an assumption and somehow model realizability is less strong. I think this is inaccurate. Given model realizability, one can construct a complete class by using the models.
- In general, the fact that no experiments are provided despite that computational efficiency is heavily advertised throughout the paper seems like a missed opportunity.
- To me, the benefit of this paper over existing results such as Zanette et al seems to only arise from the fact that the Q functions in the updates are computed via model-based methods. Aside from this, the algorithmic techniques seem fairly standard.
- The theoretical techniques do not appear to be that new. It’s more of a combination of existing techniques. While this is not a bad thing, I think it just means more focus should be put on the results.

Other suggestions
- There is a lot of discussion about why pessimism works, but this has already been explored quite extensively in past work. I think much of this can be made more concise so that the main contributions of the paper are brought forth.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written and easy to understand. As mentioned above, I feel the novelty is limited algorithmically.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents an interesting result for a model-based actor-critic method for offline RL. While the algorithm and results seem to be new, they are very similar to existing work (which was cited) without necessarily culminating significant improvements over that existing work. I also feel that several claims are unsupported.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an offline RL algorithm under the model-based setting that aims to be computationally efficient. The proposed algorithm is based on (a) natural actor critic with log-linear policy class and linear critic, and (b) model-based pessimistic policy evaluation. This paper proves that the suboptimality of the learned policy is bounded by a sum of three terms: (i) model estimation error of any function in the confidence region, (ii) policy optimization of the natural actor-critic algorithm, and (iii) the approximation error of using linear functions to approximate the critic functions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I have two major concerns about this paper -- it oversells the "computational traceability" of the algorithm and the theory of this work seems based on a few well-known components. 

1. (Computational efficiency) The algorithm involves a pessimistic policy evaluation step. Admittedly, this step is easier than pessistic planning in (Uehara & Sun, 2021). But when the confidence set is a sublevel set of TV distance, it seems unclear to me how to implement it efficiently. The authors claim that this can be achieved by projected gradient descent. But in general, the class of models might not be a convex set. I doubt that this constrained minimization oracle is hard to implement. If this oracle is not implementable, then branding this algorithm as the first algorithm that achieves computational efficiency and PAC seems problematic. Moreover, if assuming linear Bellman completeness, [Zanette et al 2021] is computationally efficient and PAC.

2. The theoretical analysis of this work seems based on a couple of well-known ingredients:
(a) the analysis of natural actor critic with log-linear function class and the sublinear convergence,
(b) analysis of sample complexity of pessimistic model-based estimation,
(c) decomposing the suboptimality as a sum of estimation error at $\pi^*$, policy optimization error, and a term that is bounded by zero thanks to pessimism. 
Each of these three components has been studied extensively in the literature. 

3. The assumptions seem a bit strange in that there are two kinds of MDP structural assumptions -- the critic of any log-linear policy can be approximated by a linear function class, and the model class is realizable. This is significantly stronger than existing literature, which usually impose only one of these two assumptions. It seems hard to find a class of transition models that (a) enables linear critics and (b) is easy for solving the pessimistic policy evaluation problem. 


Reference:

[Zanette et al 2021] Provable Benefits of Actor-Critic Methods for Offline Reinforcement Learning -- Andrea Zanette, Martin J. Wainwright, Emma Brunskill

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new model-based method for actor-critic in offline RL and analyzes its theoretical guarantees. This method is claimed to be assumption-lean and practically useful.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. The proposed model-based actor-critic algorithm in offline RL is new to the literature. 

2. The assumptions and theories are clearly stated. 

Weakness: 

1. Model-free or model-based. 

As far as I can tell, the algorithm needs the model class to have a value function that is well-approximated by linear functions. This is weird because it gets closer to the model-free setting with function approximation. What is then the benefit of model-free learning in this case? Also, is any typical assumptions for model-based algorithms needed? I only see Assumption 2 for concentrability but no well-specified model assumption is stated.  Discussion on these aspects will improve the paper. 

2. Motivation is not strong enough. Some claims on the benefit of model-based methods are vacuous. 

I did not see strong arguments for the benefit of developing a model-based method. Besides my concerns in point 1, for instance, I see that the authors argue that model-based methods need fewer assumptions to work. This may not be true because the heavy lifting is now given to specifying an appropriate model. In large-scale problems, perhaps model-free methods are more favored. In words, the motivation is not strong enough, and the authors need to provide more convincing arguments to support this study. 

3. Lack of empirical studies. 

The argument that this method is practically useful is not supported by empirical studies. As a result, this work is a pure theory paper that, however, argues its practicality. It will be strengthened if more evidence is provided regarding the practicality of the proposed method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:

This paper is clearly written. The algorithm, theory, and assumptions are clearly presented. However, the presentation of motivation and comparison to methods in the literature can be more concise and more to the point. Besides the motivation issue I mentioned, it may also help if the authors can compare their algorithm with related methods in more detail and highlight what parts are new ideas & new analysis techniques.

Quality:

This paper is of moderate quality. I feel some arguments on the motivation and the benefits of the proposed method are not strong and convincing enough. Also, arguments on practicality are not supported by empirical results. 

Novelty: 

The idea is not very original because it seems to be a combination of several ideas in the literature, and I did not see much importance or particular benefits of this combination.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper is clearly written, and all the algorithms and results are clearly stated. However, I do have concerns regarding the importance of such a new approach, because some arguments on the motivation are not very convincing (as I stated above), and those related to practicality are not well-supported due to the lack of empirical study.

content.title: Pessimistic Model-Based Actor-Critic for Offline Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Algorithms
content.abstract: Model-based offline reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved superior performance than model-free RL in many decision-making problems due to its sample efficiency and generalizability. However, prior model-based offline RL methods in the literature either demonstrate their successes only through empirical studies, or provide algorithms that have theoretical guarantees but are hard to implement in practice. To date, a general computationally-tractable algorithm for model-based offline RL with PAC guarantees is still lacking. To fill this gap, we develop a pessimistic model-based actor-critic (PeMACO) algorithm with general function approximations assuming partial coverage of the offline dataset. Specifically, the critic provides a pessimistic Q-function through incorporating uncertainties of the learned transition model, and the actor updates policies by employing approximations of the pessimistic Q-function. Under some mild assumptions, we establish theoretical PAC guarantees of the proposed PeMACO algorithm by proving upper bounds on the suboptimality of the returned policy by PeMACO.
